title: Container, k8s, CI/CD, supply chain and secrets hygiene

findings.title: scripts/backup.sh leaves the plaintext database dump behind when age encryption fails
findings.evidence:
if [ -n "${BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT:-}" ]; then
  age --recipient "$BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT" --output "$out.age" "$out"
  shred -u "$out" 2>/dev/null || rm -f "$out"
  out="$out.age"
fi
findings.why: The script runs under `set -euo pipefail` (scripts/backup.sh:10). If the `age` invocation on line 45 exits non-zero (unreachable recipient, short write, full disk, interrupted process), the shell aborts before line 46 shreds/removes the plaintext dump, so `re0auth-<stamp>.dump` — a custom-format dump containing wrapped credential DEKs and audit history — stays in the backup directory even though the operator explicitly asked for encryption. The sibling script does the opposite for exactly this failure: scripts/backup-keys.sh:117-121 wraps age in `if ! ... ; then rm -f "$out" "$out.age"; echo "age failed; the plaintext key file was removed"; exit 1; fi`. So the guard exists in this directory, just not in this script.
findings.exploit: Operator follows docs/operations.md and runs `BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT=age1... ./scripts/backup.sh /backups` where /backups is later synced to an object store (the documented replication step). age fails (e.g. a typo in the recipient or a quota-exhausted volume). The script exits 1; the operator, per backup-keys.sh's own comment, "has no reason to look for the file"; the plaintext dump is then copied to the bucket by the sync/cron step and sits there as plaintext SQL.
findings.recommendation: Mirror backup-keys.sh: `if ! age --recipient "$BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT" --output "$out.age" "$out"; then rm -f "$out" "$out.age"; echo "age failed; the plaintext dump was removed" >&2; exit 1; fi` before the shred line.

findings.title: CI/release-gate Postgres service image is a floating tag while every other image in the project is digest-pinned
findings.why: ci.yml's `test` and `probes` jobs, and perf.yml's `report` job, pull `postgres:16` by mutable tag. release.yml:19-24 runs ci.yml verbatim as the tag gate (`uses: ./.github/workflows/ci.yml`), so the release pipeline executes whatever `postgres:16` resolves to on that day, in the job that holds the repository token and the environment. This contradicts the project's own stated policy in the same files: all `uses:` actions are pinned to full commit SHAs, and the Dockerfile (Dockerfile:13, Dockerfile:49) and backup CronJob (deploy/k8s/backup/cronjob.yaml:49) pin base images by digest. The service image is the one unpinned executable in CI.
findings.exploit: A registry/account compromise or an upstream re-push of postgres:16 substitutes a malicious image. It runs on every PR and on release tags; the change is invisible to review because the mutable tag is not in the repository, and the image is handed TEST_DATABASE_URL and the workflow environment. It does not require any commit to this repo.
findings.recommendation: Pin the service image the way the other images are pinned, e.g. `image: postgres:16@sha256:<digest>` in ci.yml and perf.yml; Dependabot's existing `docker` ecosystem entry (dependabot.yml:29-32) will keep the digest current.

findings.title: Backup CronJob has no activeDeadlineSeconds: a hung pg_dump stops all future backups, silently
findings.evidence:
schedule: "*/15 * * * *"
  # Not optional. A dump that outlasts its interval would otherwise overlap the next
  # one, and the two would compete for connections against the same max_connections
  # budget the service already counts on (docs/capacity-planning.md §2).
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  # A cluster that was down for a while must not fire a burst of catch-up dumps.
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 300
findings.why: `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid` skips every new schedule while a run is still active, and the jobTemplate sets only `backoffLimit: 2` — no `activeDeadlineSeconds`, and the inline `pg_dump` (lines 69-70) has no `timeout`/`statement_timeout`. A pg_dump that blocks (lock wait, stalled I/O, a wedged sidecar, a NetworkPolicy change) runs forever, so no new dump is ever started. There is also no backup-staleness metric or alert in deploy/prometheus/re0auth.rules.yml, and the CronJob does not appear in the service's own metrics, so the promised RPO <= 15 minutes silently becomes unbounded. `startingDeadlineSeconds` and `backoffLimit` only govern missed/failed runs, not a running one.
findings.exploit: A long-running transaction or a connection-pool/network change makes the dump block mid-read. The pod stays Running; every subsequent schedule is skipped by Forbid; nothing pages because there is no signal for 'backup stopped'. Recovery is discovered only when a restore is attempted after data loss.
findings.recommendation: Add `activeDeadlineSeconds:` (e.g. 300) to the jobTemplate spec, wrap pg_dump with `timeout`/`PGOPTIONS='-c statement_timeout=...'`, and export a last-success timestamp with an alert on its age.

findings.title: .dockerignore excludes scratchpad but not the live audit workspace or generic key shapes, so they enter the `COPY . .` build layer
findings.evidence:
# The audit workspace and the other local state .gitignore excludes. The build
# needs none of it, and scratchpad/ is where audits leave probes and generated
# material — including key-shaped files — so it must not reach the build context
# or the backend stage's `COPY . .` layer (Dockerfile:42).
scratchpad
findings.why: The comment states the rule (audit workspaces and key-shaped files must not reach the `COPY . .` layer, Dockerfile:53) but the exclusion list implements only `scratchpad`. `.gitignore:62` re-includes `_audit/scriptprobe/**`, i.e. `_audit/` is the tracked audit workspace and is not in .dockerignore; neither are `AUDIT-ISSUES.md` or `docs/`. The project's own .gitleaks.toml:13-20 says `docs/security-audit-*.md` quote full JSON token responses, and the .dockerignore only excludes key-adjacent shapes `*.dump`/`*.env`/`.env` — not `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.p12`, `*.crt`, `id_*`. The file's own header (lines 1-3) says "anything copied into a layer can leak into an intermediate one".
findings.exploit: Bounded, not a direct runtime leak: the final image is `scratch` and copies only /out (Dockerfile:79-90), so this is exposure through the build context and the intermediate `build` stage layer. It becomes real when a builder is shared, `--target build` is exported, or the cache is exported to a registry (`--cache-to type=registry`) — audit artifacts and token-shaped strings land in that layer.
findings.recommendation: Add `_audit`, `AUDIT-ISSUES.md`, `docs`, and the key/cert shapes (`*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.p12`, `*.crt`, `*.jks`) to .dockerignore; better, replace `COPY . .` with an explicit list of the packages the binary needs.

findings.title: Base ConfigMap hardcodes trusted_proxies to 10.0.0.0/8; on a non-10/8 pod CIDR every client silently shares one rate-limit bucket
findings.why: clientAddr reads the declared header only when the request peer is inside TrustedProxies (clientaddr.go:78), and forwardedClient returns the peer when the rightmost hop is unparseable or itself trusted (clientaddr.go:104-110). In Kubernetes the peer of the app pod is the ingress-controller pod, whose address is the cluster's pod CIDR — not necessarily 10/8 (Calico's common default is 192.168.0.0/16; kubeadm/`--pod-network-cidr`, EKS 172.20.0.0/16, and others vary). If the CIDR does not contain that pod network, every request falls back to the ingress pod address, so all clients map to one bucket. Nothing errors or logs, and the ConfigMap comment (lines 36-42) explains the header-trust assertion but never says the CIDR must be the cluster's pod network.
findings.exploit: Not a key-forgery bypass (the configured parser takes the rightmost hop and falls back safely) but an availability failure: on a cluster whose pod CIDR is outside 10/8, a single client can spend the shared burst (rate_limit_burst = 100, configmap.yaml:23) and throttle every other client, because all requests share the ingress-pod bucket key.
findings.recommendation: Say in the comment that trusted_proxies must contain the ingress-controller pod network, and make it a per-deployment kustomize patch rather than a baseline literal; optionally add a startup warning when client_addr_header is set and the observed peer is not in trusted_proxies.

findings.title: Release image is pushed under its release tag before the Trivy gate runs; only `latest` is withheld
findings.evidence:
- id: build
        uses: docker/build-push-action@c3c9e263c25d99ce0380d002d59b67737d91b0dc # v7.4.0
        with:
          context: .
          platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
findings.why: The build-and-push step pushes the version tag (`type=ref,event=tag`, line 61-62) before the scan step at lines 100-107. If the scan fails, the workflow fails and `latest` is not created (the promotion is conditional, lines 114-119), but the version tag already exists in GHCR and is pullable. The k8s baseline selects exactly that kind of tag (deploy/k8s/base/deployment.yaml:46 `image: ghcr.io/re0auth/r0semi:v0.0.0-rc.3`), so the artifact the gate rejected is the one the shipped baseline pattern will deploy.
findings.exploit: A change passes ci.yml but adds a dependency with a HIGH/CRITICAL advisory reachable in the binary. The image is pushed as `vX.Y.Z`; Trivy then fails; the tag remains. An operator or automation that follows the baseline's tag pin (or a later manual `kubectl set image`) pulls the rejected image. The failure is only visible as a red workflow run for the tag.
findings.recommendation: Push to a staging tag or keep the image local (buildx `--load` / `outputs: type=oci`), run Trivy on the digest, and only then push the release tag — or delete the tag on scan failure. The `latest` deferral already shows the intended pattern.

findings.title: Trivy scan runs with the host Docker socket mounted inside a job holding packages:write and id-token:write
findings.evidence:
run: |
          docker run --rm \
            -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
            -v "$HOME/.docker/config.json":/root/.docker/config.json:ro \
            aquasec/trivy@sha256:ab70a02200597efa04748f210f793936eb647cbcdb0ea69cc30b226d6f5a22c7 \
            image --exit-code 1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --no-progress \
            "${{ steps.image.outputs.name }}@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}"
findings.why: The Trivy container is handed the Docker daemon socket, i.e. root-equivalent control of the runner, inside the job that also has `packages: write` (GHCR push) and `id-token: write` (Fulcio/keyless signing identity) — see release.yml:36-39. The scanner is digest-pinned, which is the right mitigation for the tool itself, but the socket is not needed: the scan target is already a registry reference with a digest (`name@sha256:...`), so Trivy can pull it directly, and the read-only docker config already provides registry credentials.
findings.exploit: A compromised Trivy image (a 0-day, or a digest whose provenance was wrong) uses the socket to run a privileged container on the runner, reads the mounted `/root/.docker/config.json` (GHCR credentials) and the job's OIDC environment, then pushes or signs arbitrary content to the project's registry.
findings.recommendation: Drop `-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock`; let Trivy pull the digest reference, or pipe `docker save` into `trivy image --input -`.

findings.title: Three alert rules keyed on generic go_*/process_* metrics carry no job selector and can fire on unrelated targets
findings.evidence:
- alert: Re0AuthGoroutineLeak
        expr: go_goroutines > 5000
...
      - alert: Re0AuthMemoryHigh
        expr: process_resident_memory_bytes > 400e6
...
      - alert: Re0AuthFileDescriptorsHigh
        expr: process_open_fds / process_max_fds > 0.8
findings.why: The file header (lines 4-7) says the expressions "name only re0auth_* series and carry no job/instance selector, so they do not bind to one scrape convention". That is true for the re0auth_* rules, but these three use generic per-target series (`go_goroutines`, `process_resident_memory_bytes`, `process_open_fds`, `process_max_fds`) which every Go process and every node-exporter/process-exporter target also exposes. Loaded into the shared Prometheus the header invites, they fire under Re0Auth names for other services, while the annotations and runbook_url point operators at Re0Auth.
findings.exploit: Operational, not adversarial: false paging on unrelated targets causes the alert set to be muted or the thresholds to be raised, so the real Re0Auth leak/OOM/FD signal is lost. The `for: 30m`/`15m` windows make it a sustained false page.
findings.recommendation: Add a deployment-supplied selector (e.g. `{job=~"re0auth.*"}`) to the three generic-metric rules, or document that they must be rewritten per deployment.

findings.title: Namespace has no Pod Security Admission labels, so the hardened pod spec is not enforced as a precondition
findings.evidence:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: re0auth
findings.why: The Deployment is carefully hardened (pod-level runAsNonRoot/runAsUser 65532/seccomp RuntimeDefault, container-level allowPrivilegeEscalation:false, readOnlyRootFilesystem:true, drop ALL), but the namespace carries no `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce` label, so nothing at the cluster level rejects a manifest that omits those fields. Any later apply (a hotfix, a kustomize overlay, an operator hand-edit, or a compromised deploy pipeline) can silently drop them; the base's own guarantees are only as strong as the next manifest applied to the namespace.
findings.exploit: A later manifest for the same namespace removes `securityContext` or adds `hostPath`/`privileged`; the API server accepts it because the namespace has no PSA enforce level. The hardened spec that reviewers approved is not what the cluster admits.
findings.recommendation: Label the namespace `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted` (plus `audit`/`warn: restricted`). The existing pod spec already complies, so this is a no-op for the baseline and a hard gate for everything after it.

findings.title: scripts/backup-keys.sh is committed mode 100644 while the documented invocation runs it directly
findings.evidence:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Back up the keys Re0Auth cannot rebuild: the KEK, the OIDC signing key, the OIDC
# token key and the audit-chain key. ...
#   RE0AUTH_OIDC_SIGNING_KEY=... RE0AUTH_AUDIT_KEY=... ./scripts/backup-keys.sh /backups
findings.why: `git ls-tree HEAD scripts/` reports `100644 blob 2ab954cf... scripts/backup-keys.sh` and `100755` for backup.sh and restore.sh, so the key-backup script has no executable bit. docs/operations.md:92 documents running it as `BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT=age1... ./scripts/backup-keys.sh /backups`, which fails with Permission denied on any fresh clone/checkout. scripts/backup-keys.sh is the only tool that archives the KEK and the three other unrecoverable keys, and docs/operations.md:133 states the database dump alone is not recoverable without it.
findings.exploit: An operator follows the documented DR steps under incident pressure; `./scripts/backup-keys.sh` fails with Permission denied; the key backup is skipped or improvised, so the encrypted database dump cannot be opened after a total loss of the deployment environment.
findings.recommendation: `git update-index --chmod=+x scripts/backup-keys.sh` and commit; add an archtest assertion that every scripts/*.sh with a shebang is mode 100755.

findings.title: Release archives embed the built SPA but do not carry the npm attribution the image deliberately includes
findings.evidence: cp config/re0auth.example.toml LICENSE NOTICE README.md SECURITY.md "dist/$$name/" || exit 1;
findings.why: The Dockerfile states the obligation explicitly: "The SPA is compiled into the very binary this image ships, so the image has the same npm notice obligation the archives carry; NOTICE covers the Go module graph only" (Dockerfile:86-90) and copies `/npm-attribution.json` into the runtime image. The archive path copies only `LICENSE NOTICE README.md SECURITY.md` (Makefile:172); the npm licence JSON is generated by the later `npm-attribution` target (Makefile:215-221, which depends on `dist`) and is only published as a sibling release asset covered by SHA256SUMS. A downloadable `re0auth_<ver>_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz` therefore ships the SPA without the licence listing, and cannot be fixed by re-running packaging without reordering the target chain.
findings.exploit: A redistributor takes an archive from a mirror (the GitHub release page is not consulted) and redistributes the embedded Svelte/SvelteKit/Tailwind code without the npm attribution; the failure is a compliance gap, not a runtime bug.
findings.recommendation: Generate the npm licence listing before packaging (or make `dist` depend on it) and copy it into each archive, as the image already does.

findings.title: Backup CronJob writes plaintext database dumps; no age encryption path is wired, unlike scripts/backup.sh
findings.evidence:
set -euo pipefail
          # 0600 from the first byte: the dump is plain SQL holding
          # credentials and audit history, and a default umask would make
          # it world-readable on the (shared) backup volume.
          umask 077
          stamp="$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"
          out="/backups/re0auth-$stamp.dump"
          pg_dump --format=custom --no-owner --no-privileges \
                  --dbname="$DATABASE_URL" --file="$out"
findings.why: The CronJob has no `BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT`/age step, so the PVC holds plaintext dumps of credential and audit data (0600, non-root, readOnlyRootFilesystem — the mitigations that do exist). docs/operations.md:125-126 explicitly accepts this (the dump is not encrypted; encrypt at the replication step or use an object store with SSE), so this is recorded as an acknowledged deployment decision rather than an unhandled gap. `scripts/backup.sh` supports age; the in-cluster path does not.
findings.exploit: Anyone with read access to the PV/CSI backend or a snapshot of it reads credential metadata and audit history in plaintext. The repository documents the compensating control (encrypt at replication / SSE).
findings.recommendation: Optionally wire age into the CronJob (recipient from a Secret, retain `*.dump.age` and cleanup patterns for it) so the in-cluster path can meet the same bar as the local script.

findings.title: .gitleaks path allowlist exempts any file matching docs/security-audit-<n>.md from every rule
findings.evidence:
[[allowlists]]
description = "Proof-of-concept output quoted in the adversarial audit reports"
paths = ['''docs/security-audit-\d+\.md''']
findings.why: gitleaks path allowlists disable all rules for matching files, and the pattern is an unanchored regex, so both `docs/security-audit-7.md` and any path containing that substring are exempt forever. The surrounding comment states the intent is narrowly to silence token-shaped output quoted from a throwaway run, and the file's own philosophy is "an allowlist that is broad enough to be convenient is an allowlist that stops catching things" — the fourth block implements that by requiring condition="AND" with a specific regex. This block does not. Recorded as residual risk, not a live leak: the exempt paths are audit reports only.
findings.exploit: A future commit (or a rename) lands a real credential in a file whose path matches `docs/security-audit-<n>.md`; the secrets job passes green on every push and on the release gate. Requires repository write access, so the privileged-actor bar is unchanged.
findings.recommendation: Scope the exemption to the rules/regexes that actually false-positive (as the last block does with `condition = "AND"`), or anchor the path pattern (`^docs/security-audit-[0-9]+\.md$`).

coverage: httpclient/outbound.go (SSRF address policy, to evaluate the NetworkPolicy egress rules)
docs/operations.md (deployment/backup invocation, to establish the exploit paths cited above)
notes: Scope read in full; no _test.go, internal/zzprobe/**, _audit/**, audit/**, AUDIT-ISSUES.md, docs/issues/** or docs/security-audit-*.md content was used as a source of any finding (only docs/operations.md, a production operator document, was cited for the documented command lines). No critical or high findings: the container runtime, the pod securityContext, the ingress/egress NetworkPolicy, the action SHA pinning, keyless signing and the release job permission split are already strong, and the SSRF guard in httpclient/outbound.go (which blocks link-local 169.254.169.254 and CGNAT 100.64/10) covers the one gap the NetworkPolicy egress IPBlock leaves. Uncertainties: (a) the sha256 digests in Dockerfile/deployment/cronjob could not be verified against upstream registries offline, and the pinned golang:1.27-alpine digest could not be checked against go.mod's `go 1.27.1` (if that base image is 1.27.0, the build would fetch a toolchain through the module proxy at build time — unverified, not reported); (b) S15-5's impact depends on the target cluster's pod CIDR and is therefore rated low/medium-confidence; (c) the DSN-in-argv exposure in scripts/backup.sh:42 and scripts/restore.sh:65,81 is explicitly documented and accepted in the scripts themselves, so it is noted here rather than filed. The release image push-before-scan (S15-6) and the docker.sock mount (S15-7) are documented decisions in the workflow comments; they are reported as residual risk with the project's own stated rationale acknowledged.
